paras: The pursuit of a Black strikebreaker on the Alton railroad was an incident in Chicago, reported in June 1903, in which union men hunted a Black non-union freight unloader employed by the Alton road. Believing that the whites meant to lynch him, the man fled and jumped into the river, and police kept him from drowning. The only account found is a short item in the Polish-language Dziennik Chicagoski, which told it as an aside in its local labor news.

In June 1903 the freight unloaders' union was in dispute with the Alton railroad, and the company was housing non-union unloaders in passenger cars. Dziennik Chicagoski blamed the union's president, printed as "Latry Curran," for calling needless strikes and reported that a committee had been chosen to reach terms with the Alton management so the unloaders could return to work. The man at the center of the incident was one of these non-union workers, described as a Negro "imported" from Missouri.

According to the paper, the man grew tired of life "in the cage" and went to rest in a freight car. Unionists saw him and organized a hunt ("obława") for the black "scab." Thinking that the whites wanted to "lynch" him, he ran and jumped into the river, where police did not let him perish.
The item names neither the man, his pursuers nor the officers, and gives no date for the incident; no report of arrests appears in the coverage.

The incident ran on page one of Dziennik Chicagoski on 27 June 1903, within the "Kronika Miejscowa" column between items on a waiters' strike, a tailors' demand for union shops and a builders' arbitration body. The paper put "scab" and "lynch" in quotation marks, presenting the lynching as the man's own fear rather than the pursuers' stated aim, and made no comment on the unionists' conduct. No English-language white paper or Black newspaper account of the incident was found.
